transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-15 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Head of ML, LatticeCloud), Tom Blake (Platform Eng), Anita Roy (CTO)

Auto-generated summary:
- LatticeCloud is evaluating options to integrate LLM features into their support and knowledge product. They want a path that minimizes changes to their LangChain/LlamaIndex-based pipelines and preserves observability.
- Main concerns: rate limits and quota handling across hosted vs dedicated; how gateway/proxy patterns fit with Redwood SDKs; ability to run private deployment (VPC) with audit logs and KMS; token-level cost visibility and tracing hooks.
- Agreed next steps: Redwood to send pilot runbook, security docs, and propose benchmark agenda; LatticeCloud to share traffic and sample prompts.

Topics:
- SDK vs Gateway sidecar adapter patterns
- LangChain and LlamaIndex connector compatibility
- Rate limiting and quota strategies (per-route, per-org, burst handling)
- Observability hooks: tracing, token cost breakdowns, latency SLO telemetry
- Private (VPC) deployment requirements and audit/KMS concerns

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I see Priya, Tom and Anita on the line, hi! we have Carlos from SE who will jump into the architecture stuff. The goal is to understand your current stack and see how Redwood could fit for hosted, dedicated, or private.

[00:12] Priya: Hi Maya, yes thanks. Quick context — LatticeCloud runs a search+RAG pipeline built on top of LangChain and LlamaIndex, mostly Python, some node services. We currently use a mix of OpenAI calls and an on-prem Triton cluster for some inference. We're trying to unify to a single inference layer for production.

[00:28] Carlos: Got it. Do you mind sharing the typical request size, average tokens per request and percent of short vs long sequences? That helps us advise on batching and quantization.

[00:37] Tom: Sure, I can summarize — median payload is 120 tokens, 80% of calls are under 300 tokens, 5% go above 2k for long document summarization. Spike pattern is unpredictable, like weekly peak during support ticket surges.

[00:50] Maya: Perfect, that explains why burst capacity and quota handling came up. Before we go deep, how opinionated do you want the integration to be? Some customers adopt our Redwood SDK directly in the LangChain llm wrapper, others front it with a gateway/sidecar to minimize app changes.

[01:05] Priya: We prefer minimal code changes initially. If there's a sidecar/gateway pattern that can accept the same LangChain outputs, that would be ideal. But we also want to keep observability and per-customer quotas.

[01:18] Carlos: Right, two common patterns: 1) SDK inline: swap your LangChain llm object to call Redwood SDK — least moving parts and supports token-level tracing and cost attribution natively; 2) Gateway/Proxy: run a lightweight adapter sidecar that translates your internal API to Redwood endpoints — good for polyglot stacks and policy enforcement, but you'll need to wire tracing headers through the proxy. Both support dedicated and private deployments.

[01:36] Anita: For security we need SSO/SAML, RBAC and audit logs. If we go private (VPC), can Redwood's control plane still offer rollouts and tracing without egressing our data?

[01:46] Maya: Yes, in Redwood Private the control plane is customer-managed in your VPC or connected via private link. We can keep inference data in your environment; the control plane only exchanges metadata and if you choose, it can be air-gapped. Audit logs and integration with your KMS/HSM for key management are supported. Carlos can show how the tracing hooks map to our console.

[02:02] Carlos: Quick note on tracing — we emit request-level and token-level telemetry. For sidecar flows we recommend propagating a trace-id header (x-redwood-trace-id) from your app to the sidecar, Redwood will preserve it and show token timing and cost breakdown in the console. If you use SDK inline, the SDK emits the trace automatically.

[02:20] Tom: That token-level cost thing — is it per-route? We need to charge back to product teams.

[02:27] Carlos: Yes, you can slice by API key, model, route, or custom tags. The console exposes token counts, latency per model, and cost estimates per call. We also provide an exportable CSV and a REST dashboard API for automation.

[02:40] Priya: LangChain/LLamaIndex — we've got chain-of-thought like prompt templates and vectorstore retrieval. Any gotchas with connectors?

[02:49] Carlos: We've done direct LangChain integrations — typically you can replace the llm provider with Redwood's llm wrapper which implements the standard LangChain interface. For LlamaIndex, we've seen two approaches: a) point LlamaIndex's llm predictor to the Redwood SDK, or b) put an adapter in front of LlamaIndex so it keeps using the same calls. Key caveat: if you rely on synchronous streaming token handlers inside LangChain, be mindful about kernel/backpressure differences if the sidecar does batching.

[03:14] Tom: Explain that backpressure thing a bit more — in our stack we stream tokens out to web clients, so latency matters.

[03:20] Carlos: Sure — Redwood's serving runtime can do continuous batching which improves throughput, but it may add a small added latency jitter if not configured. For streaming we have low-latency streaming paths; if you need sub-100ms tail latencies you might prefer Dedicated with pinned capacity and tuned batch windows. For hosted, we optimize for median latency and cost. We can tune batch thresholds per route.

[03:44] Anita: Are there rate limit primitives that we can surface to different product teams? Say Product A gets 10 req/s, Product B 1 req/s, and bursts allowed up to 5x for short windows.

[03:55] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports per-key and per-route quotas with burst windows and leaky-bucket style enforcement. We can also plug your internal policy engine into the sidecar so you can apply custom logic before requests hit Redwood endpoints.

[04:08] Priya: If we do a sidecar, will we lose out on quality controls like model rollouts and automatic fallback?

[04:14] Carlos: Not necessarily. The sidecar can still call the Redwood control plane for rollout decisions. You can configure canary rollouts, A/B routing between model variants, and automatic fallback policies (e.g., degrade to smaller model on overload). The sidecar just routes—rollout logic stays centralized.

[04:31] Tom: On the private deployment, what's the upgrade story? We need predictable maintenance windows and no surprises for compliance audits.

[04:38] Maya: For Private customers we coordinate upgrades and provide a maintenance calendar. We can run on a versioned control plane with audit logs for every change. We also provide a compatibility matrix for kernel/quantization versions so your SEs can validate before upgrading.

[04:52] Priya: About cost — how do you recommend we estimate hosted vs dedicated? We're trying to build a model to compare unit economics given our token distribution.

[05:00] Carlos: We usually do a two-step: 1) pilot to capture actual token distribution and latency needs; 2) model economics with three levers — batching (token savings), quantization/profile (model size savings), and reserved capacity discounts for Dedicated. We'll share a spreadsheet template in the pilot runbook.

[05:18] Maya: We'll include a suggested pilot size and success criteria — e.g., maintain 95th percentile latency below X ms and reduce per-token cost by Y%.

[05:27] Anita: On legal/security, we need SOC2, ISO27001 certs, attestations for BYOK via KMS, and retention controls for logs. Can you share those docs?

[05:36] Maya: Absolutely. We'll attach our SOC2 report and the BYOK KMS integration guide in the follow-up. For audit logs we support configurable retention and export to your SIEM via syslog or cloud logging.

[05:48] Tom: One implementation question — we have existing observability (OpenTelemetry) and we want Redwood traces to link into our dashboards. Is there an OTEL exporter?

[05:58] Carlos: Yes, Redwood supports OpenTelemetry: our SDKs emit OTEL spans and we can export them to your collector. For sidecar flows, the sidecar can be configured to forward spans or inject context. We recommend using your existing Collector to receive and correlate spans.

[06:12] Priya: If we run a pilot, can we test both LangChain inline and sidecar approaches in parallel? We have dev teams who prefer different paths.

[06:20] Maya: Yep, that's a common pilot pattern. We'll propose a phased pilot: week 1 integrate LangChain wrapper in a staging environment; week 2 deploy sidecar in a canary subset; week 3 run load and latency benchmarks and compare metrics.

[06:35] Tom: What about model variants — we have some internal fine-tuned models. Can Redwood accept custom model artifacts for Dedicated or Private?

[06:44] Carlos: For Dedicated and Private we support bringing your own model artifacts, subject to compatibility (PyTorch checkpoints or ONNX depending on runtime). We'll help with model onboarding — quantization/reprofile, kernel compatibility, and provide recommended config. For Hosted we typically serve models from the Redwood catalog, but we can discuss enterprise arrangements.

[07:02] Priya: One more question on quotas — can we do per-customer throttling within a single LatticeCloud org? We have an MSP-like tenant model and need per-tenant rate limits.

[07:11] Carlos: Yes, you can set per-tenant quotas via API keys or by attaching tenant-id metadata. The console and billing exports can break down usage per tenant for chargeback.

[07:22] Anita: Are there any known incompatibilities with LlamaIndex vectorstore batching? We sometimes do multi-doc retrievals that spawn multiple llm calls in parallel.

[07:31] Carlos: Parallel calls are fine; the key is to coordinate batching windows and token limits to avoid head-of-line blocking. We often suggest a slight redesign: accumulate retrieval results and use a single context window where possible, or use explicit async patterns and let the sidecar aggregate. We'll include a short pattern doc in the follow-up.

[07:49] Maya: We're tracking a couple of specific follow-ups — Carlos will draft the benchmark and pilot plan, I'll send the runbook + security attachments, Tom will share token histogram and code snippets. Anything else we should capture?

[08:02] Priya: Could you also include a sample LangChain wrapper snippet showing how to swap in the Redwood SDK? Even a minimal example will help our engineers estimate effort.

[08:11] Carlos: Sure, we'll attach code examples for LangChain and for a sidecar HTTP adapter.

[08:18] Tom: On the benchmarks, can we include an example of your dedicated p95 latency with continuous batching enabled vs disabled? We want to see real numbers with similar token distributions.

[08:27] Maya: Yep, we'll include p50/p95/p99 numbers for a couple of model families and include notes on batching windows and tail-latency tuning.

[08:36] Anita: One policy question — if a tenant exceeds quota during a surge, will you block, queue, or degrade? We need to model user experience for each.

[08:45] Carlos: You can define policy per route: hard-block, queue with retry-after, or automatic degrade to a cheaper model. Many customers do a mix — block expensive routes, degrade long-running summarizations to a cheaper model with an explicit logged fallback.

[08:58] Priya: That makes sense. Ok we should be able to take this to the execs after the pilot plan.

[09:05] Maya: Great. I'll recap the next steps at the top-level and send notes. Thanks all.
